notes:
**An audit of a section of your site now reads that section.**

Point Docket at `https://example.com/gb/en/` and it audits your UK site. Until
now it could audit somebody else's.

A large retailer's robots.txt declares one sitemap index listing 2,160 nested
sitemaps, named by locale and emitted alphabetically. Docket read the first
fifty, all of which were Estonian, and they filled its budget. A 1,000-page
audit started at the UK homepage read 999 Estonian pages and one British one —
and every finding in it was about a different country's site than the one asked
about.

Two changes. Docket now samples a sitemap index across its whole length rather
than reading the top of it, so every section of a site is represented. And when
the address you give has a path, the sitemaps that name it are read first — so
the budget is spent on the site you asked about. It is a preference, not a
filter: everything else is still crawled behind it, and an address with no path
behaves exactly as before.

Measured on that retailer, same 60-page budget: 1 page from the named section
before, 60 after.

**`--render 0` now turns JavaScript rendering off.**

Docket renders a small sample of pages in WebKit on every audit, because
several checks cannot answer honestly from static HTML alone. That is
deliberate — but `--render`'s help text still said rendering was "off unless
asked for", and passing `--render 0` rendered anyway. Rendering executes the
page's scripts, so analytics and ad pixels on the audited site fire; if you do
not want that, `--render 0` is now the way to say so, and the help text
describes what actually happens.
